name: AI for Special Education
objectives: Given a list of special education tasks, sort each task into "AI may help" or "team only", placing every IEP and 504 decision with the team

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Where AI fits, and where it does not
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Explain what AI may help with in special education and what stays with the IEP team.
This lesson builds toward: Given a list of special education tasks, you will sort each task into "AI may help" or "team only", placing every IEP and 504 decision with the team.
The Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) requires that eligible children with disabilities receive a free appropriate public education (FAPE). Under Part B, which covers ages 3 through 21, services are set out in an Individualized Education Program (IEP) developed by a team that includes the child's parents and school staff. Part C covers early intervention for infants and toddlers. Section 504 plans are a separate path for some students with disabilities.
These are individual, legal, team decisions based on evaluation and knowledge of the child. AI cannot attend the meeting, does not know the child, and can produce generic or wrong content. So AI must not write present levels, goals, services, accommodations or placement, and AI output must never be used to decide eligibility.
Where AI helps: adapting general classroom materials, creating practice at several levels, making visual supports, drafting general explanations of processes for families, and organizing your own schedule and paperwork templates (without student data).
Words to know:
- IDEA: the federal law that requires a free appropriate public education for eligible children with disabilities.
- FAPE: free appropriate public education: what IDEA guarantees eligible students.
- IEP: Individualized Education Program: the written plan of a student's special education services, made by a team including parents.
- Section 504 plan: a plan that provides accommodations for a student with a disability under a different federal law.
Official sources:
- US Department of Education: Annual Report to Congress on IDEA (Part B ages 3 through 21)
- NCLD: Individuals with Disabilities Education Act
Try it now: Make two columns: "AI may help" and "Team only". Place at least ten special education tasks from your week in the right column.
You can now draw a clear line between AI support tasks and IEP team decisions.

options: An AI tool approved by the district
A team including parents and school staff
The principal alone
The student's general education teacher alone
check.why: The IEP is developed by a team that includes parents.

check.q: A colleague asks AI to suggest which accommodations a student should get. What would you say?
options: Good idea; use its list
Ask a second AI tool to check
Accommodation decisions are for the IEP or 504 team, not AI
Use AI's list only for younger students
check.why: IEP and 504 decisions stay with the team.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Plain-language versions and chunked tasks
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI to make a plain-language version of a reading and break a task into chunks.
This lesson builds toward: Given a general reading and assignment, you will create a plain-language version and a chunked checklist with AI, comparing each with the original and fixing every dropped or changed fact.
Many students benefit from text that keeps the ideas but lowers the reading load: shorter sentences, common words, key terms explained, headings and bullet points. Prompt: "Rewrite this passage at about a 3rd-grade reading level. Keep every key fact and these vocabulary words: [list]. Use short sentences and headings. Add a box defining each vocabulary word."
Chunking breaks a multi-step task into small numbered steps with a checklist. Prompt: "Break this assignment into 5 to 8 numbered steps, one action per step, with a checkbox for each and an estimated time."
Check every version against the original: AI sometimes drops or changes facts when it simplifies. Keep the grade-level ideas; lowering the reading level should not lower the learning goal.
Step by step:
- Paste the general passage or assignment (no student info).
- Ask for the plain-language version, keeping key facts and vocabulary.
- Ask for numbered chunks with checkboxes and times.
- Compare with the original; fix dropped or changed facts.
- Keep the same learning goal.
Words to know:
- Plain language: clear writing with short sentences and common words.
- Chunking: breaking a task into small, manageable steps.
Try it now: Take a general reading and an assignment from an upcoming lesson. Make a plain-language version and a chunked checklist with AI, then compare each with the original and fix any errors.
You can now make accurate plain-language and chunked versions of class materials.

options: Short sentences and common words that keep the same ideas
A shorter text with fewer ideas
A text with no punctuation
A translation into another language
check.why: Plain language makes the text easier to read without changing its content.

check.q: AI's chunked checklist skips one step of the assignment. What do you do?
options: Use it; students will figure it out
Remove the step from the assignment
Ask students to find the missing step
Compare it with the original task and add the missing step
check.why: Checking against the original catches dropped steps and facts.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Visual supports and practice at several levels
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Create a visual schedule and two levels of practice for a lesson.
This lesson builds toward: For one general lesson, you will create a visual schedule and practice at two levels, with alt text on every image, every answer checked, and required accommodations still provided as written.
Visual schedules and supports help many students know what is coming and what to do. AI can draft the text of a visual schedule ("1. Warm-up, 5 minutes; 2. Mini-lesson...") and suggest simple icons; tools like Canva can lay it out. For images, check that pictures are clear, respectful and match the words.
Practice at several levels lets every student work on the same skill: ask AI for a set with more support (worked example first, fewer steps, word bank) and a set on level. Check every answer.
Remember that accommodations listed in a student's IEP or 504 plan must be provided as written; your materials add support for everyone but do not replace required accommodations. Check accessibility too: readable fonts, good contrast, alt text for images, and text that works with text-to-speech.
Step by step:
- Draft the visual schedule text with AI.
- Lay it out with clear, respectful icons.
- Ask for practice with more support and on level.
- Check every answer.
- Check accessibility: font, contrast, alt text, text-to-speech.
Words to know:
- Visual schedule: a picture-and-word list of what will happen, in order.
- Alt text: a short written description of an image for people using screen readers.
- Text-to-speech: technology that reads text aloud.
Try it now: Make a visual schedule for one lesson and two levels of practice for its main skill. Add alt text to any image and check every answer.
You can now create visual supports and leveled practice that make lessons more accessible.

check.q: What does a visual schedule show?
options: Students' grades
The teacher's calendar
What will happen, in order, with pictures and words
A seating chart
check.why: Visual schedules help students know what comes next.

check.q: Your two-level practice includes a word bank, but a student's IEP requires extended time. What applies?
options: Provide the extended time as written in the IEP
The word bank replaces the extended time
Ask AI which support is better
Use extended time only on tests
check.why: Required IEP accommodations must be provided as written, whatever other supports you add.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Families, privacy and team rules

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Explaining processes to families in plain words
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Draft a plain-language family explanation of a general special education step.
This lesson builds toward: Given a general special education step, you will write a one-page plain-language explanation for families, checked against your district's official materials and read by a colleague for tone.
Special education paperwork is full of terms families may not know: evaluation, eligibility, present levels, least restrictive environment, procedural safeguards. AI is good at drafting general, plain-language explanations of these terms and of what happens at each step.
Prompt: "Explain to a parent, in plain English at about a 6th-grade reading level, what happens at an annual IEP meeting: who attends, what is discussed, what they can ask, and how to prepare. Warm and respectful tone. Under 400 words." Then check it against your district's procedures and official materials, because AI may describe another state's process or get details wrong.
Keep these general. Do not use AI to write anything about a specific child. Offer translations checked by qualified speakers, and remember that your district's official procedural safeguards notice is the legal document; your explainer helps families understand it, not replace it.
Step by step:
- Choose a general step or term families ask about.
- Ask for a plain-language explanation with tone and length.
- Check it against district procedures and official materials.
- Keep it general: no specific child.
- Offer checked translations; point to the official notice.
Words to know:
- Procedural safeguards: the rights parents have in special education, explained in an official notice.
- Least restrictive environment: the IDEA idea that students with disabilities learn with peers without disabilities as much as appropriate.
Try it now: Draft a one-page plain-language explanation of one general special education step for families, check it against your district's materials, and have a colleague read it for tone.
You can now help families understand special education processes with clear, checked explanations.

check.q: What should a family explainer made with AI be about?
options: A specific child's evaluation
A general step, not a specific child
A teacher's opinion of a family
The district's budget
check.why: Family explainers stay general so no student information goes into AI.

check.q: AI's explanation of an annual IEP meeting differs from your district's materials. What would you do?
options: Share AI's version since it is clearer
Share both and let families choose
Ask AI which is right
Correct it to match the district's procedures before sharing
check.why: District procedures and official notices are the source, not the AI.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Protecting IEP and 504 information
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Apply privacy rules to special education information and AI tools.
This lesson builds toward: When staff want AI help with special education information, you will choose a safe way to get the help without sharing IEP, 504 or evaluation details, using only approved tools with minimum information.
IEPs, 504 plans, evaluations, disability information and related notes are part of a student's education records, protected by FERPA, and among the most sensitive information a school holds. Disclosing personally identifiable information from them to an outside company generally needs consent unless an exception applies.
Rules for staff: never paste IEP or 504 content, evaluation results, diagnoses, behavior plans or names into unapproved AI tools. If your district has approved an AI tool for special education work, use it only as the agreement allows, and still use the minimum information needed.
Be careful with AI note-takers and recording in meetings about students: IEP meetings should not be recorded or transcribed by unapproved tools. Your special education director and privacy officer can tell you what your district and state allow.
Step by step:
- Treat IEP, 504, evaluation and disability information as highly sensitive.
- Never put it into unapproved AI tools.
- Use approved tools only as the agreement allows.
- Use the minimum information needed.
- No unapproved recording or AI notes in student meetings.
Words to know:
- Education record: a record directly related to a student and kept by the school.
- Sensitive information: information that could cause serious harm if shared, such as disability or health details.
Official sources:
- FERPA: Protecting Student Privacy
Try it now: Write three realistic examples of special education information staff might be tempted to paste into AI, and for each, a safe way to get the same help without it.
You can now protect IEP, 504 and disability information when AI tools are in use.

check.q: Which law protects IEPs and evaluation records as education records?
options: FERPA
COPPA only
No law
Copyright law
check.why: IEPs and evaluations are education records protected by FERPA.

check.q: A teacher wants AI to rewrite a behavior plan for clarity. What is a safe way?
options: Paste the plan into a free chatbot
Remove the name but keep the diagnosis
Ask for help with a general, made-up example, or use an approved tool as the agreement allows
Email it to a friend who uses AI
check.why: Behavior plans and diagnoses never go into unapproved tools.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Team rules for AI in special education
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write five clear team rules and model them with colleagues.
This lesson builds toward: For your team, you will write five team rules for AI use in special education, with an example for each, shared with teachers, paraprofessionals and related-service providers.
Your team needs shared rules, written down. Five that cover most situations: 1) AI never writes or decides IEP or 504 content, eligibility or placement. 2) No student information in unapproved tools. 3) Every AI-made material is checked for accuracy and accessibility before students see it. 4) AI supports never replace required accommodations. 5) Family explanations are general, checked against official materials, and translated by qualified speakers.
Share them in a team meeting, with examples of what is and is not allowed. Invite questions from paraprofessionals and related-service providers, who are often left out of AI guidance.
Collect good prompts and materials in a shared folder so the time saved reaches the whole team, and review the rules each year with your special education director.
Step by step:
- Write the five rules in plain words.
- Add an example for each.
- Share in a team meeting, including paraprofessionals.
- Start a shared folder of good prompts and materials.
- Review yearly with the special education director.
Words to know:
- Paraprofessional: a school staff member who supports students and teachers, often in special education.
- Related services: supports such as speech, occupational or physical therapy that help a student benefit from special education.
Try it now: Final task: build your accessibility pack (plain-language reading, chunked checklist, visual schedule, two levels of practice), write your one-page family explanation, check everything, and write your team's five AI rules with an example for each.
You can now use AI to make special education materials more accessible while protecting students and keeping decisions with the team.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Plain-language reading and chunks A fact was dropped or changed, or the task is not chunked. A plain-language version and a numbered chunked checklist, checked against the original. Notes which errors AI made and how they were fixed. Visual schedule and practice The schedule or a practice level is missing, or answers were not checked. A visual schedule and practice at two levels, with every answer checked. Every image has alt text, and supports like worked examples or word banks are included. Family explanation It is about a specific child, or was not checked against district materials. A one-page plain-language explanation of a general step, checked for accuracy. A colleague read it for tone, and it points families to the official procedural safeguards notice. No student information Any student information appears in the pack or prompts. The whole pack uses only general or made-up material. Includes safe ways to get AI help without sharing student details. Team rules Fewer than five rules, or rules that let AI decide IEP or 504 content. Five clear rules for AI use in special education. Each rule has an example and keeps every IEP and 504 decision with the team. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Who has the final word on your district's special education rules?
options: The AI vendor
The special education director and counsel
Each teacher
The parent group
check.why: District leaders and counsel decide how rules apply locally.

check.q: You wrote five AI rules. How do you help the whole team use them?
options: Share them with teachers, paraprofessionals and related-service providers, with examples
Email them to principals only
Keep them in your own files
Post them once and never review them
check.why: Everyone who works with students needs the rules and examples.
